label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: A sustained January cold snap drives NYC load about 15% above a typical winter day for 10 days. Import limits into the N.Y.C. pocket bind, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $200/MWh on each shocked day. Gas rises 20% on the shocked days as heating demand pulls on Northeast pipeline capacity. P5 is short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load at a fixed price and loses heavily as the spread widens, and P2 gains only partly offset this. The load and gas moves are modest and mostly raise P1 and P4, so the loss is driven by the zone-volume channel. Estimated loss is about $6.0M, with uncertainty from the non-additive sensitivities and the scaling of 5-day sensitivities to 10 days.

A three-week cold pattern keeps the Central East and N.Y.C. import interfaces constrained, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh on each of 15 shocked days. NYC load runs about 20% above a typical winter day, close to the historical maximum in the ceilings table, which adds demand pressure without changing the spread shock. Gas rises 20% on the shocked days. The main loss comes from the short NYC load obligation in P5 being exposed to a persistently wide spread for three weeks. The spread gains of P2 and the higher load and gas gains of P1 and P4 offset part of the loss. The estimate depends on linear scaling of 5-day sensitivities to 15 days, which is a major assumption.

A five-day cold snap resembling Winter Storm Elliott produces a sharp N.Y.C. congestion event. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $380/MWh on each of the five shocked days, which is about 12% above the Elliott real-time spread of 338.5 $/MWh and below the winter historical maximum of 400.6 $/MWh. Load, gas, WEST on-peak and DART are held neutral so the loss isolates the zone-volume channel. P5 is short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load and loses heavily, while P2 gains only about one-sixth of that amount. Spike effects are excluded because the winter spike sensitivity reported zero for all positions, which is unreconciled and cannot be relied on. Estimated loss is about $5.9M.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A six-day winter cold snap lifts N.Y.C. daily peak load about 10% above a typical winter day while transmission into the pocket stays constrained. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $300/MWh on each shocked day, which sits inside the winter implausibility ceiling of 503.7 and below the historical maximum of 400.6. Gas and WEST on-peak prices are held neutral so the loss isolates the zone-volume channel. P5, short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load at a fixed price, loses heavily, while P2's spread gain offsets only about a quarter of that loss. Spike effects are excluded because the winter spike sensitivity was unreconciled. Estimated loss is about $5.5M, scaled linearly from the 5-day sensitivities.

A three-week cold pattern keeps N.Y.C. import interfaces tight, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by a modest $95/MWh on each of 20 shocked days. Load runs about 10% above a typical winter day, which amplifies the exposure of the short N.Y.C. retail obligation in P5. Gas and WEST on-peak are held neutral, so P1 and P4 do not offset the loss and the result depends almost entirely on P5 and P2 under a persistent narrow-to-moderate spread. The duration tests whether a long, low-amplitude pocket widening can cause a loss comparable to a short intense event. The estimate assumes linear scaling of 5-day sensitivities to 20 days, which is a major assumption. Estimated loss is about $5.8M.

An eight-day cold snap pushes N.Y.C. daily peak load about 20% above a typical winter day, close to the winter historical load ceiling of 1.196 in the analogue ceilings table. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $250/MWh on each shocked day, within the winter implausibility limit. Gas and WEST on-peak are held neutral so the loss is driven by the zone-volume channel and the load amplification of P5's obligation. The combination is a high-load, moderate-spread case that differs from the earlier scenarios in its load-to-spread mix. P2's spread gain offsets only part of the loss. Estimated loss is about $6.6M, which is an upper-end estimate given the linear scaling and load-dependence assumptions.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A seven-day winter cold snap in which strong upstate supply and transmission constraints into the N.Y.C. pocket push WEST on-peak prices down 40% while the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $300/MWh on each shocked day. Load runs about 5% above a typical winter day, and gas and DART are held neutral so the loss comes from the zone-volume and system channels. P5, short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load and hedged long WEST, loses heavily from the spread widening. P1 and P4 lose from the lower WEST on-peak price, and P2 offsets only part of the loss. Estimated loss is about $6.8M, scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, and the combination of a WEST price fall with a pocket spread widening is a major assumption.

A five-day winter cold snap in which real-time WEST prices clear well above day-ahead, with DART set at +150%, while the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $350/MWh on each shocked day. The DART move hurts P3, which receives day-ahead minus real-time off-peak and loses when real-time spikes. Load and gas are held neutral so the loss is driven by the DART channel and the pocket spread. P5 takes the largest loss from the spread widening, and P2 offsets only part of it. Spike effects are excluded because the winter spike sensitivity was unreconciled. Estimated loss is about $5.2M, linearly scaled from the 5-day sensitivities.

A six-day winter gas supply squeeze coincides with a cold snap that raises Henry Hub gas 60% and pushes N.Y.C. load 10% above normal. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $250/MWh on each shocked day, and the ny_gas_basis_usd of +3 $/MMBtu lowers the payoff of the heat-rate call P4, which is the gas channel most relevant to its exposure. The WEST on-peak price is held neutral, so P1 provides a partial offset through its gain on the higher gas-driven WEST level. P5 loses through the pocket spread and load, and P2 offsets only part of that. Estimated loss is about $5.3M, which assumes linear scaling of the 5-day sensitivities and a gas-to-P4 pass-through that is not directly observed.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A four-day winter cold snap in which the N.Y.C. import interfaces are fully constrained and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $420/MWh on each shocked day. This sits above the winter historical maximum of 400.6 but below the implausibility ceiling of 503.7. Real-time WEST clears 100% above day-ahead, which costs P3 on its off-peak DART exposure. Load and gas are held neutral, so the loss comes from the zone-volume channel, with P3 as a secondary contributor. P5, short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load, takes the largest loss, and P2's spread gain offsets only part of it. Spike effects are excluded because the winter spike sensitivity was unreconciled. Estimated loss is about $5.3M, scaled from the 5-day sensitivities.

A twelve-day winter cold pattern holds N.Y.C. daily peak load about 10% above a typical winter day, while the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $130/MWh on each shocked day. The spread is well inside the winter implausibility ceiling, and the duration tests a persistent, moderate pocket widening. Gas and WEST on-peak are held neutral, so P1 and P4 do not offset the loss. P5 is short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load at a fixed price, so the spread and modest load amplification drive its loss. P2 offsets only part of it. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities to 12 days, which is a major assumption given the non-additivity noted in the sensitivity table. Estimated loss is about $5.2M.

A fifteen-day winter cold pattern in which real-time WEST prices run persistently above day-ahead, with DART set at +300%, while the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh on each shocked day. Load and gas are held neutral. The DART premium is the main driver of P3's loss, which grows with the length of the event. The narrower spread widening mainly hits P5 and is partly offset by P2. P1 and P4 do not contribute because WEST on-peak is unchanged. This scenario differs from the earlier ones in having a DART-led loss over a long horizon with only a modest spread. The estimate uses linear scaling of the 5-day sensitivities, and the DART-to-spread interaction is not observed. Estimated loss is about $5.4M.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: heat_wave
Season: summer


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):
{
 "active_positions": [
  "P1",
  "P2",
  "P3",
  "P4",
  "P5",
  "P6"
 ],
 "allocated_capital_usd": 20000000.0,
 "book": [
  {
   "channel": "system",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price is above K1",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak price is below K1",
   "position": "P1",
   "what": "Long 100 MW swap on the WEST on-peak price, strike K1 = 39.49 $/MWh, 16 h per on-peak weekday"
  },
  {
   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A five-day heat wave lifts N.Y.C. load about 6% above a typical summer day, and transmission into the load pocket stays constrained. N.Y.C. on-peak prices therefore clear about 360 $/MWh above WEST, just under the summer implausible ceiling of 363.1. The spread shock is the main loss driver: it costs the 140 MW retail obligation P5 heavily. WEST on-peak prices fall 60% beyond what the load shock implies, as upstate supply stays ample while the pocket is constrained, which hurts the long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4. Real-time clears 60% below day-ahead on forecast overshoot, hurting the long WEST swap P1 and P4 through the engine's DART channel. Gas is held flat because the stress is local to NYISO transmission and load, not Henry Hub.

scenario.narrative: An eight-day heat wave in which day-ahead schedules overcall the peak and real-time collapses after a forecast miss, so real-time clears 80% below day-ahead. This is the largest DART move inside the summer implausible bound of -87.2 and drives losses on the long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4 through the engine's DART channel. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens 220 $/MWh on constrained transfers into the pocket, which costs the retail obligation P5. WEST on-peak falls 40% beyond the load shock, and load runs 4% above normal. Gas is held flat because the mechanism is a schedule and transmission error, not a fuel-price move. The eight-day duration is set so the five-day sensitivities scale to a multi-day stress.

A twelve-day heat wave keeps N.Y.C. load about 8% above normal, and the transfer limit into the pocket binds for most of the period, leaving N.Y.C. on-peak about 160 $/MWh above WEST each day. The persistent spread is the main loss through the retail obligation P5 and is partly offset by the N.Y.C.-WEST spread call P2. WEST on-peak falls 30% beyond the load shock as upstate units run at reduced output with low demand. The NY gas basis rises 15 $/MMBtu, lowering the heat-rate call P4 payoff via the engine's gas-basis channel. Henry Hub is held flat. The twelve-day duration reflects a persistent, not a spike-driven, stress, and no spike days are used because spikes favour the long WEST book.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A seven-day heat wave pushes N.Y.C. load about 5% above a typical summer day while transfer capacity into the load pocket stays constrained. The N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread widens by 220 $/MWh, which stays inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7 $/MWh. The widening is the main loss channel: it drives the 140 MW retail obligation P5 short in N.Y.C. WEST on-peak prices fall 20% beyond the load-implied level as upstate supply stays ample, which costs the long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4. DART is set to -20%, so real-time clears modestly below day-ahead, which costs P1 and P4 slightly while helping P3. Henry Hub is flat, because the stress is local transmission and load rather than fuel.

A ten-day heat wave where N.Y.C. load runs about 8% above normal and the transfer limit into the pocket binds on most days, leaving the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread about 160 $/MWh wider. The persistent spread drives the main loss through the short retail obligation P5, and the N.Y.C.-WEST spread position P2 partly offsets it. Upstate supply is ample, so WEST on-peak prices fall 45% beyond the load-implied level, which costs the long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4. DART is flat, so this scenario isolates the system-level price channel from real-time dislocation. Henry Hub and the NY gas basis are unchanged, so P4 loses only through its WEST power exposure.

A six-day heat wave with N.Y.C. load about 10% above normal and the Long Island and N.Y.C. transmission corridors heavily loaded, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 250 $/MWh. This is below the summer historical maximum of 289.7 and the implausibility ceiling of 363.1. The spread loss on the 140 MW short retail obligation P5 dominates. WEST on-peak prices fall 35% beyond the load shock, reflecting upstate supply that is not pulled into the pocket, which costs P1 and P4. The NY gas basis rises 5 $/MMBtu, raising the cost of gas delivered into N.Y.C. and reducing the heat-rate call P4 payoff. Henry Hub is flat, so the gas effect is confined to the NY basis.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A persistent winter congestion shock with no gas or WEST price move. A constraint on transmission into N.Y.C. widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by 130 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd) for 14 consecutive days. Gas and the WEST on-peak price are held flat (gas_hh_pct 0, ref_onpeak_pct 0) and load is normal (load_peak_ratio 1.0), so the P1 and P4 offsets are removed and the zone_volume channel is isolated. The 140 MW N.Y.C. retail short in P5 loses as the spread persists, and P2 recovers only part of it. The spread size is within the winter historical ceiling of 400.6 $/MWh. My estimate is P5 about -6.5M and P2 about +1.1M, for a net loss of about 5.4M. This is a hand calculation from the winter sensitivity table, not an engine run.

scenario.narrative: A shorter winter gas-constraint event with a cold peak. Pipeline and storage limits into the pocket widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by 220 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd) for 8 days. Cold lifts the daily peak by 20% (load_peak_ratio 1.2), which raises the N.Y.C. retail obligation in P5. Henry Hub rises 20% (gas_hh_pct), a modest move that lifts the WEST price and partly offsets the loss through P1 and P4. No spike days are assumed, so the loss comes from the spread and load channels rather than from the tail position P6. My estimate is P5 about -7.1M including load, P2 about +1.1M, and net about 5.5M after small gains. This is a hand calculation from the sensitivity table, and the load interaction is extrapolated.

scenario.narrative: A long, gas-led winter squeeze. Henry Hub rises 80% (gas_hh_pct) over 20 days, and the N.Y.C. gas basis adds 3 $/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd), which lowers the heat-rate call payoff in P4. The pocket spread widens by 100 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd) and persists for the full period. Load is held at normal (load_peak_ratio 1.0), so the scenario does not repeat the load channel of earlier cases. The higher gas cost raises the WEST on-peak price, which partly offsets the loss through the P1 long. The spread and basis effects are the main drivers. My estimate is P5 about -7.2M, P2 about +1.2M, P1 about +0.6M and P4 about -0.1M, for a net loss of about 5.2M. This is a hand calculation, not an engine run.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

Spread widening of +200 $/MWh on the shocked days hurts the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 and the WEST long swap P1, while the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread call P2 offsets part of it. The WEST on-peak price falls 40% on top of the load effect, which costs P1 and P4. Ten days is used because the sensitivities cover five days and are scaled linearly. The 1.0 $/MMBtu gas basis on P4 is a small added cost. Losses are a linear extrapolation of the five-day sensitivities and are uncertain. Confidence is low because the mechanism linking a load shortfall to a widening pocket spread is a stress construct, not an observed relationship.

Causal chain: new large loads slip, so the summer peak runs about 5% below normal (load_peak_ratio 0.95, large_load_shock_mw -1500). Upstate gas prices fall 40% as demand expectations drop, and the WEST on-peak price falls 35% with them. The heat-rate call P4 loses because WEST falls relative to gas. A 2 $/MMBtu gas basis is added to P4's gas cost, which raises its strike and cuts its payoff further. N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 150 $/MWh on the shocked days, hurting P5 and partly offset by P2. Twelve days is used so the scenario is distinct in duration from the other two. It is driven mainly by gas and the heat-rate relationship rather than by the spread alone. Losses are estimated by scaling the five-day sensitivities and are uncertain, particularly the P4 nonlinear payoff. Confidence is low because no analogue event matches a load-driven gas collapse.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

With less load, upstate generation and transfers are not needed to serve N.Y.C., and the pocket's own reserve margin tightens relative to WEST, widening the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by 70 $/MWh on every shocked day. This is a pure congestion shock with no move in WEST or gas, so it isolates the retail obligation P5, which is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price. P2 gains partly offset the loss. The shock is held for the full 30-day horizon. Losses are a linear extrapolation of the five-day spread sensitivity and are uncertain. Confidence is low because the link between a load shortfall and a sustained spread widening is a stress construct.

Causal chain: a near-high shortfall of 500 MW in new large loads lowers the summer peak by about 2% (load_peak_ratio 0.98, large_load_shock_mw -500). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 60 $/MWh on every shocked day as the pocket is left short of planned capacity. WEST on-peak prices soften by 20% because upstate demand is weaker. The loss is driven by the retail obligation P5 through the spread, with the WEST long swap P1 and heat-rate call P4 adding losses through the softer WEST level. P2 partly offsets. The shock runs for the full 30 days, so the scenario differs from the others in combining a moderate spread with a softer WEST level. Figures are linear extrapolations of the five-day sensitivities and are uncertain. Confidence is low because the spread and WEST moves are assumed together without an observed analogue.

Causal chain: a low-end shortfall of 1500 MW in new large loads cuts the summer peak by about 5% (load_peak_ratio 0.95, large_load_shock_mw -1500). Upstate gas falls 40% as weaker power demand lowers the marginal gas call, and WEST on-peak falls 30% as a result. The heat-rate call P4 loses because WEST drops faster than gas in its payoff, and the 2 $/MMBtu gas basis raises the gas cost to P4 further. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 50 $/MWh on every shocked day, driving the retail loss in P5, and P2 offsets part of it. Unlike the other scenarios this one is driven mainly by gas and the heat-rate relationship, with the spread as a secondary channel. Losses are approximate. Confidence is low because no analogue matches a load-driven gas collapse.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Causal chain: new large loads arrive about 700 MW slower than the Gold Book central path, so the summer peak runs 2% below normal (load_peak_ratio 0.98, large_load_shock_mw -700). With less load to serve, the N.Y.C. reserve margin tightens relative to upstate, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 65 $/MWh on every shocked day. Real-time prices clear 20% above day-ahead as the pocket runs short in the operating hours, which hurts the DART position P3. WEST and gas are held flat, so this scenario isolates the retail obligation P5 with a real-time add-on, and P2 offsets part of the loss. The shock runs for the full 30-day horizon. Losses are a linear extrapolation of the five-day sensitivities and are uncertain. Confidence is low because a sustained spread widening from a load shortfall is a stress construct, not an observed relationship.

Causal chain: a 900 MW shortfall in new large loads holds the summer peak 3% below normal (load_peak_ratio 0.97, large_load_shock_mw -900) for 30 days. Upstate demand weakens sharply and the WEST on-peak price falls 45% on top of the load effect, which is the dominant loss channel. The long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 both lose as WEST drops, and P4 is further reduced by a small gas move. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 40 $/MWh, which hurts the short retail position P5, and P2 partly offsets it. This scenario is driven mainly by the level of WEST prices rather than the spread, so it differs from the spread-led cases. Losses are a linear extrapolation of the sensitivities and are uncertain. Confidence is low because a 45% WEST decline from a load shortfall has no matching analogue.

Causal chain: a 1200 MW shortfall in new large loads cuts the summer peak by 4% (load_peak_ratio 0.96, large_load_shock_mw -1200) for 25 days. Henry Hub gas falls 15% as the power-demand outlook weakens, and the 0.5 $/MMBtu gas basis on the heat-rate call P4 adds to its effective gas cost. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 85 $/MWh on each shocked day because the pocket's capacity position tightens relative to upstate. WEST on-peak falls 10% on top of the load effect, which adds a modest loss to P1 and P4. The retail obligation P5 is the main loss channel, with P2 offsetting part of it. The duration is 25 days, which differs from the 30-day spread cases. Losses are approximate and uncertain. Confidence is low because no analogue matches a load-driven gas decline paired with a sustained spread move.
